fixed.before: Therefore, if so many and such great marvels, which they call *mēchanēmata* [contrivances], are produced from God's creation by those using human arts, so that people who do not know them suppose them to be divine (whence it came about that in a certain temple, with lodestones placed in the floor and in the vault in proportion to their size, an iron image hung in the middle of the air between the two stones, as if by the power of a deity, to those who did not know what was above and below; something of which kind, as we have already said, could also have been done by a craftsman in that lamp of Venus with the asbestos stone); if the works of magicians, whom our scripture calls poisoners and enchanters, could exalt demons so far that a famous poet thought he was in keeping with men's beliefs when he said of a certain woman who was powerful in such an art: “She promises with her spells to set free the minds of whom she will, but to send harsh cares on others, to halt the water in the rivers and turn the stars back; and she stirs up the ghosts of the night: you will see the earth bellow beneath her feet and the ash trees come down from the mountains”: how much more is God able to do things that are incredible to unbelievers, but easy for his power, since he himself created the force of stones and of other things, and the talents of men who use them in wonderful ways, and the angelic natures more powerful than all earthly living things, with a wonderful power surpassing all wonders, and with the wisdom of working, commanding and permitting, using all things as wonderfully as he created them.

fixed.before: But let us return to the speech put in the mouth of the Jew, in which the mother of Jesus is described as having been driven out by the carpenter who was betrothed to her, having been convicted of adultery and bearing a child by a certain soldier named Panthera; and let us see whether those who made up the tale of the adultery of the virgin with Panthera, and of the carpenter who drove her out, did not fabricate all this blindly in order to overthrow the miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit. For because of the story's being so very extraordinary they could have falsified it in some other way, and not, as it were, involuntarily agreed that Jesus was not born of an ordinary human marriage. And it was consistent that those who did not assent to the miraculous birth of Jesus should invent some lie; but that they did this unconvincingly, keeping the point that the virgin did not conceive Jesus by Joseph, was a manifest lie to those able to listen and to expose fabrications. For is it reasonable that he who dared so much on behalf of the human race, so that, as far as lay with him, all Greeks and barbarians, expecting divine judgement, might turn away from wickedness and do everything in a way pleasing to the Creator of the universe, should have had no miraculous birth, but of all births the most lawless and most shameful? I will speak as to Greeks, and especially to Celsus, who, whether he holds Plato's views or not, at any rate cites them: would he who sends souls down into human bodies thrust the one who was to dare so much, to teach so many, and to turn many people away from the outpouring of wickedness, into a birth more shameful than any, not even bringing him into human life through a lawful marriage? Or is it more reasonable that each soul, being introduced into a body according to certain secret principles (I say this now in the manner of Pythagoras and Plato and Empedocles, whom Celsus often named), is introduced according to its merit and its former character? It is likely, then, that this soul too, which came to dwell in human life to the greater benefit of many people (so that I may not seem to beg the question by saying 'all'), needed a body not only outstanding among human bodies but also better than all.

fixed.before: That he foreknew such things by a divine impulse, and that the account of those who think the man a wizard is unsound, is shown by what has already been said; but let us consider the following too. Wizards (and I consider them the most ill-starred of men), some by resorting to the torturing of images, some to barbarous sacrifices, some to chanting a spell or applying an ointment, claim to alter what is fated; and many of them, when brought to trial on charges, have confessed to being skilled in such things. But he followed the decrees of the Fates, and foretold that these things must come to pass, and he foreknew them not by wizardry but from what the gods revealed. And when he saw among the Indians the tripods and the wine-pourers and all the things that they said came in of their own accord, he neither asked how they contrived them nor wished to learn, but he praised them and did not think fit to imitate them.

fixed.before: The devil answered: “Adam, what are you saying to me? It is on your account that I was thrown out from there. When you were formed, I was thrown out from the presence of God and sent outside the company of the angels. When God breathed the breath of life into you, and your face and likeness were made in the image of God, Michael brought you and had you worshipped in the sight of God, and the Lord God said: ‘Behold, Adam, I have made you in our image and likeness.’

fixed.before: A physical explanation, and not an inelegant one, is enclosed in these impious myths. For they meant that the heavenly, highest, ethereal, that is fiery, nature, which generates all things by itself, lacks that part of the body which needs union with another for procreation. And they meant Saturn to be the one who maintains the course and revolution of periods and seasons. This god has that very name in Greek: for he is called *Kronos*, which is the same as *chronos*, that is, a span of time. And he was called Saturn because he was sated (*saturaretur*) with years; for he is imagined to have been in the habit of devouring his own children, because age consumes the spans of time and is insatiably filled with the years that have passed. He was bound by Jupiter, so that he should not have unrestrained courses, and so that [Jupiter] might tie him with the bonds of the stars. But Jupiter himself, that is, 'helping father' (*iuvans pater*), whom in the other cases we call *Iovis*, from helping (*iuvando*), is called by the poets 'father of gods and men', and by our ancestors 'best and greatest', and indeed 'best', that is, most beneficent, before 'greatest', because it is a greater thing, and certainly more pleasing, to benefit everyone than great wealth—
